title: I Spent 24 Hours With Early Humans (300,000 years ago)

narration.text: Night. Three hundred thousand years ago.

narration: Fardin is hiding behind a rock. And he is not alone.

narration.text: Something is circling the camp. Then comes the sound.
Spotted hyenas. And Fardin just realized something terrible.

narration: The people around this fire can't see him. But he has no idea if the hyenas can.
But to understand how he got here, we need to go back a few hours.

narration.text: This is Fardin. Normal guy. Red hoodie. One very unusual watch.

narration: Turn the dial, and he falls back through time as a ghost.
Nobody there can see him or hear him. He can only watch.
Tonight, he set the dial further back than ever.

graphics.sub: Time Ghost · invisible in the past

narration: Three hundred thousand years.
In the next twenty four hours, he'll see three things that changed how we think about our species.
A hunt with stone tipped spears.
A rock trick so clever, it lasted two hundred thousand years.
And by tonight, the strangest discovery of all: who else was out there.

graphics.title: IN THE NEXT 24 HOURS
items: A rock trick used for 200,000+ years

narration: Dawn. Fardin is standing on a dry, rocky hillside, in what will one day be Morocco. There are no countries yet, no farms, and no cities anywhere on Earth.
Scientists call this place Jebel Irhoud.
In 2017, researchers announced that human fossils found here are about three hundred thousand years old.
They are the oldest known fossils of our own species. Homo sapiens.

graphics.label: years old: the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils

narration: And there they are. A small group, waking up beside a cave.

narration.text: Fardin's first thought? They look... surprisingly normal.

narration: And he's right, mostly. Their faces were a lot like ours. But the back of the skull was longer and lower.
Their brains were about as big as ours, but shaped differently. The rounder brain shape we have today seems to have appeared later.
Here's a way to feel how long ago this is.
Squeeze the whole story of our species into one twenty four hour day. Farming doesn't show up until about eleven PM.
The pyramids? Eleven thirty eight. Almost everything in your history books happens in the last half hour.

graphics.caption: Our species' story as one 24-hour day

narration: And forget the Sahara you know. At times, North Africa was much greener, with grasslands, lakes and rivers.

narration.text: Gazelles and other grazing animals roamed here. Fardin tries waving at a man walking right past him.

narration: Nothing. Not even a blink. He really is a ghost here.
But that's fine. Because the hunt is about to begin. And it's nothing compared to what happens after dark.

graphics.text: CLIMATE SWUNG BETWEEN WET AND DRY

narration: Mid morning. A few hunters grab their spears and head out, and Fardin tags along, three steps behind.
Archaeologists dug up many animal bones at Jebel Irhoud, and the most common by far belonged to gazelles. Many carry cut marks from stone tools.

graphics.label: The most common animal bones at Jebel Irhoud, many with stone-tool cut marks

narration: Here's the problem. A gazelle can sprint at up to around eighty kilometers an hour. No human can catch one.

narration.text: So the hunters creep in low. Quiet. Downwind. Closer.
And closer.

graphics.label: top sprint speed of a gazelle. Humans top out near 45.

narration.text: Now!

narration: The spear flies, and misses. The whole herd explodes away.

narration.text: Fardin is laughing so hard he forgets he's invisible. Then he remembers, and laughs even louder.

narration: But the hunters don't give up. They spread out. Patient. Working as a team. Hunting like this takes planning, and trust.

narration.text: On the next try, one throw finds its mark.

narration: Some stone points from this site look like they were made to be fixed onto wooden shafts. Did these hunters throw their spears, or stab up close? Scientists are still debating that.
And the strangest part of their day hasn't happened yet.
Back at camp, it's lunchtime. And Fardin learns a rule fast. Nothing gets wasted.
They slice the meat with stone flakes, sharp enough to cut through hide.
Then someone grabs a heavy rock, places a leg bone on a flat stone, and smashes it open.

narration.text: Inside is marrow. Soft, fatty, and full of energy. They scoop it out, and eat it. Raw.
Fardin looks like he's about to be sick.

narration: But to them, this is a treat. Humans and our ancestors had been cracking bones for marrow for more than a million years.

graphics.label: years that humans and our ancestors have cracked bones for marrow

narration: Did they cook any of it? Possibly. Some flint tools here were burned in fire, and that's actually how scientists dated the site.
But how often people cooked their food this long ago is still uncertain.
They almost certainly ate plants too. Roots, seeds and fruits. But plants rarely survive this long, so most of the menu is lost.

narration.text: Fardin decides to skip lunch.

narration: Good call. Because later tonight, he'll find out these people were not alone on this planet.

graphics.label: years: age of burned flint tools, dated using the heat they received

narration: Afternoon. In the shade of the cliff, an older man sits down with two stones. Fardin sits right next to him.
This, it turns out, is high technology.
He doesn't just smash the rock. He shapes it, chip by chip, as if he's planning several moves ahead. Every strike has to land at just the right angle.

narration.text: Then, one precise strike...

narration: and a ready made blade pops off, sharp along its edges.
Archaeologists call this the Levallois technique. The toolmaker had to picture the final tool inside the stone, before it existed.
Methods like this were used across Africa and beyond for more than two hundred thousand years.

graphics.label: Shape the stone first, then strike off a ready-made tool
years that prepared-core methods like this were in use

narration: Fire is part of life here too. Burnt flint and bone tell us these people used it. Fire meant warmth, light, protection, and maybe cooked food.
And far away in Kenya, at a site called Olorgesailie, people from around this same time carried black obsidian rock from as far as ninety kilometers away.
Ninety kilometers is roughly two marathons, on foot. They also collected red and black pigments. Was that trade between groups? Some scientists think so. Others aren't sure.

graphics.label: how far obsidian was carried at Olorgesailie, around 320,000 years ago

narration: Either way, these were people who planned ahead, remembered and connected. Just with very different gear.
Then the sun starts to sink. And Fardin is about to find out why nobody here wanders off after dark.
Sunset. The group pulls in close around the fire. Fardin finally relaxes.

narration.text: Big mistake.

narration: Out in the dark, shapes are moving.
Across Africa, early humans shared the land with lions, leopards and spotted hyenas.
And here we are. This is the moment from the beginning.

graphics.label: lions, leopards and spotted hyenas all lived alongside early humans in Africa

narration: The hyenas circle closer. The adults rise, spears ready.

narration.text: Someone grabs a burning branch, and hurls it toward the dark.
The eyes back away.

narration: Fire probably helped keep predators at a distance. It's one of the oldest safety tricks our species has.
Fardin's heart is pounding. Then he remembers, he's the only one here who can literally walk through a wall.

narration.text: He's still not going out there.

narration: Late at night, inside the cave, people lie down on beds of grass. Fardin tries one. Surprisingly comfy.
This part isn't a guess. At Border Cave in South Africa, scientists found grass bedding about two hundred thousand years old.
It was laid on top of ash, possibly to keep crawling insects away.

graphics.label: years old: grass bedding laid over ash
graphics.source: Border Cave, South Africa · study published 2020

narration.text: Fardin lies awake, staring out at the stars. Then his watch buzzes, with one last fact. The biggest one.
These people were not the only humans on Earth.

narration: Around this time, there were Neanderthal ancestors in Europe, and mysterious Denisovans in Asia, known mostly from their DNA.
A small brained species called Homo naledi lived in South Africa. Another kind of archaic human lived in what is now Zambia. And on the island of Java, probably some of the last Homo erectus.
At least five different kinds of humans may have shared the planet at the same time.

graphics.label: kinds of humans may have shared the planet

narration.text: Today, only one is left. Us.

narration: Scientists are still working out why. Much later, some of those other humans even had children with our ancestors. That's why many people alive today carry a little Neanderthal or Denisovan DNA.

graphics.label: Neanderthal DNA in most people with non-African ancestry

narration: Dawn is coming. Fardin's twenty four hours are almost up. His watch starts to glow.

narration.text: But the dial is spinning the wrong way.

narration: Next time, Fardin lands in ancient Egypt, right in the middle of building the Great Pyramid.

graphics.sub: The Great Pyramid · about 4,500 years ago

narration: Subscribe, or Fardin stays lost in time.

graphics.sub: or Fardin stays lost in time
